key_insight: The paper argues that representational convergence in medical foundation models is driven more by self-supervised learning than by clinical supervision. In other words, models become more similar because of how they are trained at scale, not simply because they were trained on medical labels or clinical objectives.
problem_solved: It addresses the open question of whether different medical image encoders truly learn a shared underlying representation, and whether claims of interchangeability are supported by robust similarity measures.
method: Runs a controlled comparison across 18 image encoders and 7 text encoders, all open-weight and executed locally.
Examines models spanning a wide scale range, from 7M to 27B parameters.
Dissects how training signal type and model scale affect representational similarity using careful, more robust evaluation rather than relying on fragile similarity metrics alone.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this clarifies that model similarity in medical AI cannot be assumed from size or clinical supervision alone. It helps guide better model selection, benchmarking, and evaluation of whether encoders are truly interchangeable in downstream medical workflows.
visual_elements: A side-by-side flow diagram comparing self-supervised vs clinically supervised training pipelines.
A heatmap of representational similarity across the 18 image encoders and 7 text encoders.
A parameter-scale axis showing models from 7M to 27B with clustering patterns overlaid.
An icon-based summary showing 'training signal', 'scale', and 'clinical usefulness' as three factors affecting convergence.
paper_title: Self-supervision drives representational convergence in medical foundation models more than clinical supervision
paper_authors: Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh, Sebastian Ziegelmayer, Mahshad Lotfinia, Lisa Adams, Sven Nebelung
